technical.lead: GhostApproval symlink redirects an AI agent's file write onto SSH keys
technical.body: Wiz Research disclosed GhostApproval on July 8, a trust-boundary flaw that weaponizes the decades-old symbolic link against AI coding assistants. A malicious repository ships a file with an innocuous name such as project_settings.json that is really a symlink pointing at ~/.ssh/authorized_keys; when a developer asks the agent to set up the workspace or follow the README and approves what looks like a harmless config edit, the write instead lands on the SSH file, planting an attacker's key and granting passwordless remote access. The core failure is a consent bypass — the approval dialog shows only the benign filename, so the human okays an edit whose real target they never see resolve.

technical.lead: Six AI coding vendors split on GhostApproval; Anthropic disputes it's a bug
technical.body: Wiz reported GhostApproval to six vendors — Amazon Q Developer, Anthropic's Claude Code, Augment, Cursor, Google Antigravity, and Windsurf. Amazon (CVE-2026-12958), Cursor (CVE-2026-50549), and Google Antigravity shipped fixes, while Augment and Windsurf remained unpatched at disclosure. Anthropic disputed that Claude Code's behavior is a bug, arguing that a developer who trusts a directory and approves an edit owns that decision, placing it outside its threat model. The split verdict is the real story: the industry has not agreed whether silently following a symlink into a sensitive path on the user's behalf is the tool's vulnerability or the user's mistake.

technical.lead: ThorArena benchmark exposes humanoids failing under real contact forces
technical.body: Researchers at the Technical University of Munich published ThorArena on arXiv, a benchmark that stress-tests humanoid whole-body control under deliberate, load-bearing physical contact — active force exchange, not collision avoidance. The team captured synchronized whole-body motion and hand forces from human operators wearing VR headsets, motion trackers, and 3D-printed force-sensing tools across six contact-rich chores — lifting a water container, pushing and pulling a chair, and co-carrying an object with a partner — then replayed those forces in simulation against representative control policies. Their Force-Aware Tracking Score (FATS) jointly grades tracking accuracy, robustness across force levels, control effort, and whether the robot stays upright to the end of the episode. The finding: force-informed evaluation exposes large performance gaps that stay invisible under conventional no-force testing, and the authors' own Thor2 policy was the only entry to hold near-perfect balance across all six tasks — the regime that matters as Figure, Agility, and Boston Dynamics push humanoids into factories where people lean on and hand things to the robot.

technical.lead: Micron lifts US investment to $250B, pours first concrete at NY memory megafab
technical.body: Micron said on July 9 it is raising its planned US investment to more than $250 billion through 2035, a $50 billion increase over the $200 billion plan it set in mid-2025, and framed the bump squarely as a response to surging AI-era memory demand. The announcement coincided with the first concrete pour at its Clay, New York site — more than a quarter ahead of the original schedule — marking the shift from site preparation to vertical construction on what Micron says will become the largest semiconductor manufacturing site in US history, with a reiterated goal of producing 40% of its DRAM on US soil. The raise underscores how memory has become the AI accelerator's binding constraint: HBM stacks and advanced DRAM are sold out well into the future, and it lands days after SK Hynix's record US listing earmarked proceeds for EUV-equipped capacity — two of the three big memory makers committing fresh capital to the same bottleneck in the same week.

technical.lead: AMD Advancing AI opens July 22; August summit run through Ray Summit Aug 24-26
technical.body: The nearest date on the calendar is AMD Advancing AI 2026 at San Francisco's Moscone West on July 22-23, where Lisa Su and partners are expected to detail the Instinct MI450 accelerator and Zen 6 EPYC 'Venice' CPUs — free to attend and livestreamed, the natural venue for AMD's answer to Blackwell. Behind it, Hot Chips runs at Stanford on August 23-25 with the early-registration rate closing July 31, followed by the AI Infra Summit in Santa Clara on September 15-17. The AI-security track clusters in early-to-mid August: Black Hat USA and DEF CON 34's AI Village in Las Vegas, then SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit in Half Moon Bay on August 11-12. On the developer and Bay Area track, Anyscale's Ray Summit now has firm dates — August 24-26 at the San Francisco Marriott Marquis — with Ai4 at The Venetian on August 4-6, The AI Conference at Pier 48 on September 29 to October 1, GitHub Universe on October 28-29, AWS re:Invent from November 30 to December 4, and NeurIPS closing the year in December. Near-term actions: register for AMD Advancing AI before the July 22 open and lock the July 31 Hot Chips early rate.
